essays.stem: Describe the main parts of the nail and say what each part does.
essays.modelAnswer: The matrix is under the skin at the base of the nail. It makes new cells, so it is where the nail grows from, and damage to it can spoil the nail for good. The lunula is the pale half-moon at the base of the nail; it is the part of the matrix we can see. The nail plate is the hard part made of keratin that we file and polish; it has no nerves or blood vessels. It sits on the nail bed, which has many blood vessels, so a healthy nail looks pink. The eponychium is the living skin at the base of the nail, and the cuticle is the thin dead tissue that it leaves on the nail plate. Together they seal the base of the nail against germs. The hyponychium is the skin under the free edge, which also seals out germs. The nail walls are the folds of skin at the sides, and the free edge is the part that grows past the fingertip.
markingPoints: Matrix makes new cells (growth); lunula is the visible part of it
Nail plate: hard keratin, no nerves or blood vessels
Nail bed: under the plate, with blood vessels
Eponychium and cuticle: seal at the base against germs
Hyponychium, nail walls and free edge described correctly

essays.stem: Explain how a nail grows, and describe the things that can change how fast or how well it grows.
essays.modelAnswer: New nail cells are made in the matrix at the base of the nail. As new cells form, they push the older cells forward. The cells fill with keratin and harden, and the nail plate slides forward over the nail bed towards the fingertip. Fingernails grow faster than toenails, so a whole toenail takes much longer to grow out than a fingernail. Nails often grow faster in young people, in warm weather and on the hand a person uses most. Good health and a balanced diet with enough protein, vitamins, iron and water help nails grow strong. Illness, a high fever, poor diet, some medicines and stress can slow growth or cause marks such as Beau's lines. Injury to the matrix can make the nail grow back misshapen or not at all. Harsh treatment, such as heavy filing, biting, or soaking often in remover, weakens the nail plate even though it does not change the speed of growth.
markingPoints: New cells are made in the matrix and push the nail forward
Cells harden with keratin; the plate slides over the nail bed
Toenails grow more slowly than fingernails; age, season and hand used
Health, diet, illness and medicines affect growth and can cause marks
Injury to the matrix, and harsh treatment, damage the nail

essays.stem: Describe the layers of the skin and explain why a nail technician needs to understand them.
essays.modelAnswer: The skin has three main layers. The epidermis is the outer layer. It has no blood vessels, and its top part is made of flat, dead cells that are shed all the time and protect the body from germs, water loss and harm. The dermis is under the epidermis. It holds blood vessels, nerves, sweat glands, oil glands, hair follicles and fibres that keep the skin firm and stretchy. Under the dermis is the subcutaneous layer of fat, which protects and insulates the body. A nail technician needs to know this because the skin is the client's barrier against infection. If tools cut through the epidermis, germs can enter the dermis and blood. This is why we never cut live skin, and why we do not treat over cuts or broken skin. Knowing about nerves and blood flow helps us use the right massage pressure. It also helps us understand dry skin and allergic reactions to products.
markingPoints: Epidermis: outer, protective, no blood vessels
Dermis: blood vessels, nerves, glands and fibres
Subcutaneous fat layer
Broken skin lets germs in, so no cutting of live skin or working over cuts
Links to massage pressure, dry skin or reactions

essays.topic: Bones of the hand and foot
essays.stem: Name the bones of the hand and the foot, and explain how this knowledge helps when you give a hand or foot massage.
essays.modelAnswer: In the hand, the wrist is made of small bones called carpals. The palm is made of five long bones called metacarpals. The fingers and thumb are made of phalanges: three in each finger and two in the thumb. In the foot, the ankle, heel and back of the foot are made of the tarsals. The middle of the foot is made of five metatarsals, and the toes are made of phalanges, like the fingers. Knowing where the bones and joints are helps the technician massage safely. I use firm pressure on the soft, fleshy parts such as the palm, the muscles of the forearm and the sole, and lighter pressure over bony areas, the knuckles and the ankle bones. I move each joint gently and only as far as is comfortable. I take extra care with clients who have stiff or painful joints, such as arthritis, and I do not massage over a recent injury or fracture.
markingPoints: Hand: carpals, metacarpals, phalanges
Foot: tarsals, metatarsals, phalanges
Firm pressure on fleshy areas, lighter over bones and joints
Gentle joint movements within comfort
Care with arthritis; no massage over recent injury

essays.stem: Give examples of nail conditions that can be worked on in the salon and conditions that need referral to a doctor. Explain how you decide.
essays.modelAnswer: Some nail conditions are not infections and do not spread, so a careful service can go ahead. Examples are white spots (leuconychia) from small knocks, fine ridges, bitten nails (onychophagy), hangnails, mild peeling, and Beau's lines that are growing out. These can often be helped by gentle filing, buffing, cuticle oil, a ridge-filling base coat and good aftercare. Other conditions need a doctor. These include fungal infection (onychomycosis), with thick, yellow, crumbly nails; paronychia, with red, swollen, painful skin and perhaps pus; a green or dark patch under a lifted nail; a nail lifting badly from the bed (onycholysis) with no clear cause; spoon-shaped nails; and a new dark streak in the nail. To decide, I ask questions and look in good light. If there are signs of infection, pain, swelling, pus, bleeding or a change I cannot explain, I do not treat. I explain kindly without diagnosing, refer the client to a doctor and record it.
markingPoints: Gives at least two conditions that can be worked on
Says how those can be helped (gentle filing, buffing, oil, ridge filler)
Gives at least two conditions that need referral
Signs that mean stop: infection, pain, swelling, pus, unexplained change
Explains kindly, does not diagnose, refers and records

essays.stem: Compare bacteria, viruses and fungi. Give a nail or skin example of each, and say how the salon stops them spreading.
essays.modelAnswer: Bacteria are tiny single cells. Many are harmless, but pathogenic bacteria cause disease. In nail work, bacteria can cause paronychia, an infection of the skin fold around the nail, and green patches under lifted artificial nails. Viruses are even smaller and can only grow inside living cells. Warts and verrucas on the hands and feet are caused by a virus and spread by contact. Fungi include moulds and yeasts. They like warm, damp places, such as between the toes, and cause athlete's foot and fungal nail infection (onychomycosis). The salon stops them spreading by not treating infected areas and referring the client. Staff wash their hands before and after each client. Tools are cleaned, then disinfected as the maker says, or sterilised, and stored closed. Single-use items are used once only, fresh towels are used for each client, and foot spas and surfaces are cleaned and disinfected between clients. Feet are dried well between the toes.
markingPoints: Bacteria described, with a correct example
Viruses described, with a correct example (warts or verrucas)
Fungi described, with a correct example (athlete's foot or onychomycosis)
No treatment over infection; referral
Hand washing, cleaning then disinfecting or sterilising, single-use items, fresh towels

essays.stem: Explain what these nail products do: acetone and non-acetone remover, nail primer, acrylic liquid and powder, and gel polish. Give one safety point for each.
essays.modelAnswer: Acetone is a strong solvent. It dissolves polish and soak-off gel quickly, but it dries the skin and nails and is very flammable, so it is kept closed and away from heat. Non-acetone remover is gentler and is often used where the maker says acetone would harm an enhancement, but it is still flammable and must be kept away from flames. A nail primer prepares the natural nail so that the enhancement product sticks to it. Some primers can burn the skin and eyes, so a tiny amount is applied only to the nail plate, and eye protection is used if the maker says. In an acrylic system, the liquid (monomer) is mixed with the powder (polymer) and it hardens on the nail. The liquid has strong fumes, so good ventilation is needed, and it must not touch the skin. Gel polish hardens only when cured under the UV or LED lamp the maker says. Under-cured gel or gel on the skin can cause an allergy, so it is kept off the skin.
markingPoints: Acetone and non-acetone remover: what they do, flammable and drying
Primer helps adhesion; can burn skin and eyes, use sparingly
Acrylic: liquid monomer and powder polymer harden; fumes and ventilation
Gel cured only under the lamp the maker says
Keeps products off the skin to prevent allergy

essays.stem: Explain what overexposure to nail products is, the signs of an allergic reaction, and how a technician prevents reactions in clients and in herself.
essays.modelAnswer: Overexposure means coming into contact with a product too often or for too long, by touching it, breathing its fumes or dust, or getting it in the eyes. Repeated skin contact with products such as gel, primer and acrylic liquid can make a person allergic. The allergy can build up slowly, and once it starts it often lasts for life. Signs include redness, itching, swelling, small blisters, or dry, cracked skin around the nails or on the fingers, and sometimes on the face or eyelids. Breathing fumes or dust can cause headaches, sore eyes or breathing problems. To prevent this, I keep products off the skin by working neatly and leaving a small gap at the cuticle and sides. I cure gel fully with the correct lamp, as the maker says. I never touch products with bare hands, I wear gloves, use extraction or good ventilation, wear a dust mask when filing, and close bottles after use. If a reaction happens, I stop, remove the product safely, record it and refer to a doctor.
markingPoints: Defines overexposure: too much or too long contact, by touch, breath or eyes
Repeated contact can cause a lasting allergy
Signs: redness, itching, swelling, blisters, cracked skin; breathing effects
Prevention: neat application, full curing, gloves, ventilation, mask, closed bottles
If a reaction occurs: stop, remove safely, record, refer

essays.stem: Describe how you keep a nail work area safe from fumes, dust and fire, and explain why the safety data sheet (SDS) is important.
essays.modelAnswer: Nail products give off fumes, and filing makes fine dust, so the work area must be well ventilated. Where the Centre has one, I use a table extraction unit that pulls fumes and dust down and away from my face and the client's. I keep only the small amounts I need on the desk, use bottles with closing lids, and close them after each use. I wear a dust mask when filing enhancements, and gloves, and I wipe the desk often so that dust does not build up. Many products, such as acetone, remover and acrylic liquid, are flammable. I store them labelled, closed and in a cool place, away from heat, sunlight and flames, and nobody smokes in the salon. Pads soaked in product go into a lined metal bin with a closed lid, emptied every day. The SDS tells me the hazards of each product, how to store and handle it, the PPE to use, how to deal with a spill, and the first aid. I read it before using a new product.
markingPoints: Ventilation and extraction for fumes and dust
Small amounts, closed bottles, desk wiped
Dust mask and gloves
Flammable products stored safely; no smoking; soaked pads in a lidded metal bin
SDS gives hazards, storage, PPE, spills and first aid; read before use

essays.stem: Describe how you carry out a nail and skin analysis before a nail service, and how you use the results.
essays.modelAnswer: I wash my hands and ask the client to cleanse hers. I ask about her health, medicines, allergies, work and hobbies, past nail services, and any problems she has noticed. Then I look at the nails and skin in good light, one hand at a time. I check the nail shape and length, the colour of the nail beds, and the thickness and strength of the nail plate. I look for ridges, white spots, peeling, splitting, lifting, bitten edges, discolouring or a dark streak. I check the cuticles, hangnails, and the skin for dryness, cuts, warts, redness or swelling. I decide whether there are any contraindications. If there are signs of infection or a change I cannot explain, I do not treat and I refer the client to a doctor. If the nails are healthy or have a minor condition, I choose a suitable service and products, such as a warm oil manicure for dry, brittle nails. I write the results on the record card, agree the plan and give aftercare advice.
markingPoints: Asks about health, medicines, allergies, lifestyle and past services
Examines nails in good light: shape, colour, strength, marks and lifting
Examines skin and cuticles for dryness, cuts, warts, redness or swelling
Identifies contraindications and refers where needed
Chooses a suitable service, records the results and agrees the plan

practical1.title: Nail and skin analysis of the group, with a labelled nail structure poster
practical1.brief: As a group, make a large labelled poster of the nail and the skin around it, and a chart that sorts common nail conditions into 'can be worked on' and 'refer to a doctor'. Each member draws and labels part of the poster (for example matrix, lunula, nail plate, nail bed, eponychium, cuticle, hyponychium, nail walls and free edge) and writes what that part does in their own words. Then work in pairs, on members who agree: each member carries out a full nail and skin analysis of a partner's hands, and of the feet if the partner agrees, in good light. Fill in an analysis sheet for each partner: health questions, nail shape, colour, strength, any ridges, spots, lifting or peeling, skin and cuticle condition, any contraindications, and the service you would choose and why. Photos show only hands, feet and the work, never faces. Hand in the poster, chart and analysis sheets with the photos.
materials: Large poster paper or card, markers and rulers
Reference pictures of nail conditions from the Centre's textbooks
Nail and skin analysis sheets and pens
Good lighting or a magnifying lamp
Cotton pads and remover, if polish must come off for the analysis
photos: The finished labelled nail structure poster
The chart of nail conditions sorted into 'work on' and 'refer'
Each member working on their part of the poster
A partner's hands being examined in good light
Close-up of nails during analysis (hands only)
The completed analysis sheets, laid out together
checklist: Labelled their part of the nail structure correctly and explained what it does
Placed nail conditions correctly as 'can be worked on' or 'refer'
Washed hands and asked suitable health and lifestyle questions
Examined nails and skin in good light, one hand at a time
Recorded shape, colour, strength, marks and skin condition accurately
Spotted any contraindication and said they would refer it, without diagnosing
Chose a suitable service and gave a sensible reason based on the analysis
safety: Wash hands before and after touching a partner's hands or feet
Do not touch broken skin or a suspected infection; note it and tell the assessor
Remove polish only in a ventilated area, with remover kept closed and away from heat

practical2.title: Safe use of nail products: product safety cards and a warm oil manicure for dry nails
practical2.brief: As a group, choose four or five nail products the Centre uses, such as acetone remover, non-acetone remover, cuticle softener, nail primer and a gel or acrylic product. Each member reads the label and safety data sheet for one product and makes a product safety card: what it does, its hazards, the PPE to use, how to store it, what to do with a spill, and first aid. Present the cards to the group. Then, in pairs on members who agree, each member gives a warm oil manicure suited to dry or brittle nails found in the analysis: check the hands, warm the oil as the maker says and test it on the inside of your wrist, soak the nails, push back the cuticles gently, massage the hands, buff gently and finish with a ridge-filling base coat or cuticle oil. Store every product correctly at the end. Photos show only hands, products and the work area.
materials: Four or five nail products with their labels and safety data sheets
Card, markers and pens for the safety cards
Manicure oil, a warming bowl and warm water
Disinfected cuticle pushers, new files, buffers and orange sticks for each client
Ridge-filling base coat and cuticle oil
Towels, gloves, a lined metal bin with a lid and a sharps box
photos: The finished product safety cards, one per member
A member presenting a card to the group
Products stored closed and labelled in the correct place
The wrist test on the warmed oil
The nails soaking in warm oil
The hand massage in progress (hands only)
The finished nails, and the cleaned station
checklist: Took correct facts from the label and SDS: use, hazards, PPE, storage, spills and first aid
Explained their card clearly to the group
Checked the client's hands for contraindications first
Warmed the oil as the maker says and tested it on the inside of the wrist
Pushed back cuticles gently without cutting live skin
Massaged with correct movements and comfortable pressure
Buffed gently without thinning the nail plate and finished neatly
Closed and stored all products correctly and put soaked pads in the lidded metal bin
safety: Read the SDS and follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Keep flammable products closed and away from heat and flames; work in a ventilated area
Never warm oil over a flame; test it on the wrist before it touches the client
Keep primer, gel and acrylic liquid off the skin and eyes; rinse with clean water if splashed and report it
